questions.q: Why does this course prefer double over float for prices and financial calculations?
options: float is deprecated in modern C++
double cannot hold negative numbers
double's extra precision avoids compounding rounding error across many calculations
float cannot be used with the + operator
questions.explain: double is a 64-bit floating-point type with more precision than float's 32 bits, which matters when rounding error compounds across millions of calculations.

questions.q: What is the correct way to compare two double values for 'equality' in C++?
options: Use == directly, since doubles compare exactly like integers
Compare the absolute difference against a small tolerance, e.g. std::abs(a - b) < 1e-9
Cast both to int first, then use ==
Doubles cannot be compared at all
questions.explain: Floating-point values accumulate rounding error, so direct == comparison is unreliable. Comparing the absolute difference against a small tolerance is the standard approach.

questions.q: What does marking a variable const accomplish in C++?
options: It makes the variable global
It tells the compiler the variable cannot be reassigned after initialization, catching accidental changes as errors
It forces the variable to be a double
It deletes the variable at the end of the program automatically
questions.explain: const marks a variable as not reassignable after it's initialized. The compiler will flag any attempt to change it, and it documents intent for readers.

questions.q: What is the key difference between enum class and a plain, old-style enum?
options: enum class values are scoped (e.g. Side::Buy) and don't silently convert to int
enum class can only hold one value ever
There is no difference; they are interchangeable in all contexts
Plain enum is newer and enum class is deprecated
questions.explain: enum class requires qualifying each value with the enum's name and prevents the implicit conversion to int that a plain enum allows, making it safer for representing things like order side or trade status.

questions.q: In `for (double f : fills) { total += f; }`, what kind of loop is this?
options: A while loop
A range-based for loop that iterates each element of fills directly
An infinite loop
A switch statement
questions.explain: This is a range-based for loop: it walks every element of the fills collection directly, without the programmer managing an explicit index.
